qft-canonical-quantization.title: From classical fields to operator-valued distributions

questions.q: Canonical quantization of a free real scalar field $\phi$ imposes which equal-time commutation relation between $\phi$ and its conjugate momentum $\pi = \dot\phi$?
choices: $[\phi(t,\vec x), \pi(t,\vec y)] = i\hbar\,\delta^3(\vec x - \vec y)$.
$[\phi(t,\vec x), \pi(t,\vec y)] = 0$ — fields commute at equal times.
$\{\phi(t,\vec x), \pi(t,\vec y)\} = i\hbar\,\delta^3(\vec x - \vec y)$ — anticommutator.
$[\phi(t,\vec x), \phi(t,\vec y)] = i\hbar\,\delta^3(\vec x - \vec y)$.
questions.hint: The canonical pairing comes from the Poisson bracket $\{\phi(\vec x),\pi(\vec y)\}_{\mathrm{PB}} = \delta^3(\vec x - \vec y)$ promoted by the Dirac quantization rule $\{\cdot,\cdot\}_{\mathrm{PB}} \to \tfrac{1}{i\hbar}[\cdot,\cdot]$. Anticommutators belong to fermions, not scalars.
questions.explain: $[\phi(\vec x),\pi(\vec y)] = i\hbar\,\delta^3(\vec x-\vec y)$ is the field-theoretic analogue of $[\hat q,\hat p] = i\hbar$ in QM, with the Kronecker delta upgraded to a Dirac delta. Choice 1 would mean classical commuting variables — no quantum theory. Choice 2 is the canonical relation for fermion fields ($\{\psi_\alpha,\psi^\dagger_\beta\} = \delta_{\alpha\beta}\delta^3$), forced by spin-statistics. Choice 3 mistakes which pair gets the delta — $[\phi,\phi]$ at equal times vanishes.

questions.q: Mode-expanding $\phi(x) = \int \frac{d^3p}{(2\pi)^3 2E_p}\bigl[a_p e^{-ip\cdot x} + a_p^\dagger e^{ip\cdot x}\bigr]$ for a real scalar resolves Klein-Gordon's negative-probability problem. Select all true statements about why this works.
choices: Both branches $E = \pm\sqrt{p^2+m^2}$ get reinterpreted: $a_p^\dagger$ creates a positive-energy quantum at momentum $\vec p$; the would-be negative-energy mode becomes the $a_p^\dagger$-coefficient with $e^{+ip\cdot x}$.
The Hamiltonian $H = \int d^3p\,E_p\,a_p^\dagger a_p + (\text{const})$ is bounded below by $0$ on the vacuum once the constant is normal-ordered away.
The conserved charge $Q = \int d^3x\,j^0$ is no longer interpreted as a probability density but as particle-minus-antiparticle number, so its sign flexibility is physically reasonable.
Negative-energy plane waves are projected out by hand; only positive-energy modes appear in the expansion.
questions.hint: Three of these capture the actual reinterpretation; one is a common misreading. The negative-energy modes are not deleted — their coefficients become creation operators for positive-energy quanta with reversed-sign convention.
questions.explain: (0) Both signs of $E$ are kept, but only one sign of energy appears in the spectrum: $a_p^\dagger$ raises energy by $E_p>0$. (1) Normal ordering subtracts the zero-point divergence $\sum_p \tfrac12 E_p$; what remains is a non-negative number operator. (2) The current $j^\mu$ is a charge current (number minus antinumber weighted by $U(1)$ charge), so $j^0$ being indefinite is exactly correct. (3) is the pre-QFT misreading — modern formalism keeps both branches and reinterprets, it does not project.

questions.q: Order the conceptual steps that take a classical Klein-Gordon field $\phi$ to a quantized operator-valued distribution acting on Fock space.
items: Define a vacuum $|0\rangle$ by $a_p|0\rangle = 0$ for all $p$, and build multi-particle Fock-space states by acting with $a_p^\dagger$.
Promote $\phi(x)$ and its conjugate momentum $\pi(x) = \dot\phi(x)$ from c-number functions to operators on a Hilbert space.
Impose $[\phi(t,\vec x),\pi(t,\vec y)] = i\delta^3(\vec x-\vec y)$, all other equal-time commutators zero.
Mode-expand $\phi$ in plane waves and read off coefficients $a_p, a_p^\dagger$ that satisfy $[a_p,a_q^\dagger] = (2\pi)^3 2E_p\,\delta^3(\vec p-\vec q)$.
questions.hint: The flow goes: choose a thing to promote, write down its bracket, decompose it spectrally, then identify the spectrum. The vacuum is named only after creation/annihilation operators are in hand.
questions.explain: (1) Promotion to operators is the conceptual leap. (2) The canonical bracket fixes the algebra. (3) Mode expansion diagonalizes the free Hamiltonian and exhibits the harmonic-oscillator structure. (0) The vacuum is the kernel of all annihilation operators, and Fock space is built from it. Out of order: e.g. trying to define $|0\rangle$ before having the $a_p$ algebra is circular — there's nothing to annihilate.

questions.q: For a free scalar field, the $n$-particle subspace of Fock space is:
choices: $\mathcal{H}_1^{\otimes n}$ — all tensor products with no symmetry imposed.
$\mathrm{Sym}^n\mathcal{H}_1$ — symmetric tensor products, since $a_p^\dagger a_q^\dagger|0\rangle = a_q^\dagger a_p^\dagger|0\rangle$ by $[a_p^\dagger,a_q^\dagger]=0$.
$\Lambda^n\mathcal{H}_1$ — antisymmetric tensor products (fermion case).
The unsymmetrized tensor product $\mathcal{H}_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes \mathcal{H}_1$ but restricted to $n!$-permutation-equivalent states.
questions.hint: Bosons commute. Compute $a_p^\dagger a_q^\dagger - a_q^\dagger a_p^\dagger$ from the canonical commutation relations; this fixes which symmetry the multi-particle states inherit.
questions.explain: $[a_p^\dagger,a_q^\dagger] = 0$ for bosons forces $a_p^\dagger a_q^\dagger|0\rangle = a_q^\dagger a_p^\dagger|0\rangle$, i.e. the two-particle state is symmetric under particle exchange. Iterating, the $n$-particle subspace is exactly $\mathrm{Sym}^n\mathcal{H}_1$. (2) is the fermion case (anticommuting $b_p^\dagger$). (3) is empirically wrong: bosons obey Bose-Einstein statistics, not classical Maxwell-Boltzmann.

questions.q: For a Dirac fermion, the same construction with anticommuting $b_p^\dagger$ gives Fermi-Dirac statistics. What does $\{b_p^\dagger,b_p^\dagger\} = 0$ imply for the two-particle state $b_p^\dagger b_p^\dagger|0\rangle$?
choices: It equals $2\,(b_p^\dagger)^2|0\rangle$ — twice the bosonic counterpart.
It vanishes — the Pauli exclusion principle: two identical fermions cannot occupy the same single-particle state.
It equals $|0\rangle$ — the operators cancel.
It is undefined — anticommuting operators don't admit squaring.
questions.hint: Apply the anticommutator $\{b_p^\dagger, b_p^\dagger\} = 2(b_p^\dagger)^2$ to the vacuum, and use the explicit $\{b_p^\dagger, b_p^\dagger\}=0$ from the canonical anticommutation relations.
questions.explain: $\{b_p^\dagger,b_p^\dagger\} = 2(b_p^\dagger)^2 = 0$ forces $(b_p^\dagger)^2 = 0$. So $b_p^\dagger b_p^\dagger|0\rangle = 0$ identically — there is no two-fermion state with both quanta in the same momentum and spin state. This is the Pauli exclusion principle, derived from Lorentz invariance + microcausality + half-integer spin via the spin-statistics theorem (Pauli 1940), not assumed.

questions.q: Match each Fock-space concept on the left to its precise structural description on the right.
right: Tells you which particle types use commutators (integer spin) vs anticommutators (half-integer spin) — the only choice consistent with Lorentz invariance and microcausality.
Direct sum $\bigoplus_{n\ge 0}\mathcal{H}^{(n)}$ over $n$-particle subspaces; for bosons each $\mathcal{H}^{(n)}=\mathrm{Sym}^n\mathcal{H}_1$, for fermions $\Lambda^n\mathcal{H}_1$.
Cyclic vector annihilated by every $a_p$ (or $b_p$) and every fermion antiparticle annihilator; spans the $n=0$ subspace.
questions.hint: Two of these objects are spaces / vectors (a Hilbert space and a single state); one is an operator (eigenvalue gives a count); one is a foundational theorem (statement, not object). Sort by category first.
questions.explain: (0)→2: Fock space is the direct sum over all particle numbers. (1)→3: the vacuum is the no-particle state, killed by every annihilation operator. (2)→1: the number operator's eigenvalue on a multi-particle Fock state is the total particle count. (3)→0: the spin-statistics theorem is the Lorentz-invariance-plus-microcausality constraint that pins which spins go with commutators vs anticommutators.

questions.q: The Feynman path integral expresses the transition amplitude $\langle\phi_f|e^{-iHT}|\phi_i\rangle$ as:
choices: $\sum_{\mathrm{classical}}e^{iS_{\mathrm{cl}}/\hbar}$ — a sum over classical solutions only.
$\int\mathcal{D}\phi\,e^{iS[\phi]/\hbar}$ — a sum over ALL field histories $\phi(x)$ matching the boundary conditions, weighted by $e^{iS}$.
$\int\mathcal{D}\phi\,|S[\phi]|^2$ — a sum weighted by the squared classical action.
$e^{iS_{\mathrm{cl}}[\phi_f-\phi_i]/\hbar}$ — exactly the classical-action exponential, with no integration.
questions.hint: Feynman's insight was that quantum mechanics sums over every conceivable history, not just stationary ones. The phase weighting is what makes the sum converge to the classical answer in the $\hbar\to 0$ limit, by stationary-phase / saddle-point argument.
questions.explain: $\int\mathcal{D}\phi\,e^{iS[\phi]/\hbar}$ sums over every $\phi(x)$ — classical solutions, near-misses, wildly non-classical paths — weighted by the phase $e^{iS}$. As $\hbar\to 0$, stationary phase localizes the integral on $\delta S = 0$ (the Euler-Lagrange equation), recovering classical mechanics. (0) Restricting to classical paths drops the quantum content entirely. (2) $|S|^2$ would be a probability weight, not a phase, and would not interfere. (3) Drops the integration that makes it quantum.

questions.q: Find the error in this attempted derivation of the classical limit: "Stationary phase tells us that as $\hbar\to 0$, the path integral $\int\mathcal{D}\phi\,e^{iS[\phi]/\hbar}$ is dominated by paths with $S[\phi] = 0$, since only zero-action paths contribute non-oscillatory terms. Therefore in the classical limit, the system follows the path of zero action."
steps: Note that as $\hbar\to 0$, the phase $S/\hbar$ oscillates rapidly except where $S$ has special behaviour.
Conclude that the dominant contribution comes from paths where $S[\phi] = 0$.
State: the classical limit is the path of zero action.
questions.hint: Stationary phase looks for points where the EXPONENT'S DERIVATIVE vanishes, not where the exponent itself vanishes. Reread the integrand: which combination of derivatives is what makes the phase locally non-oscillatory?
questions.explain: Step 2 confuses 'zero action' with 'stationary action'. Stationary phase localizes $\int e^{iS/\hbar}$ on the configurations where $\delta S/\delta\phi = 0$ — the Euler-Lagrange equation — NOT on $S = 0$. A path with $S[\phi]\ne 0$ but $\delta S = 0$ (a non-trivial classical solution) is the dominant contribution. The classical principle is 'stationary action' for a reason. The fix: replace 'paths with $S=0$' by 'paths satisfying $\delta S/\delta\phi = 0$'.

questions.q: For Euclidean signature $t \to -i\tau$, the action becomes $iS \to -S_E$ where $S_E[\phi]>0$ is the Euclidean action. The path integral becomes:
choices: $\int\mathcal{D}\phi\,e^{-S_E[\phi]/\hbar}$ — a Boltzmann-weighted sum, identical in form to a statistical-mechanics partition function $Z = \sum_\phi e^{-\beta H[\phi]}$.
$\int\mathcal{D}\phi\,e^{+S_E[\phi]/\hbar}$ — divergent without further regulation.
Undefined — Euclidean continuation breaks unitarity, so the path integral has no analogue.
$\int\mathcal{D}\phi\,\cos(S_E[\phi]/\hbar)$ — a real-valued sinusoidal weight.
questions.hint: The Wick rotation $t = -i\tau$ replaces an oscillatory weight by an exponential decay weight when $S_E > 0$. Compare to the Gibbs distribution in classical statistical mechanics: what role does $S_E/\hbar$ play, and what role does $\beta H$ play?
questions.explain: $iS \to -S_E$ converts the oscillating weight $e^{iS/\hbar}$ to a decaying weight $e^{-S_E/\hbar}$, identical in form to a Boltzmann factor with $\beta\hbar \leftrightarrow 1$. This is the duality between Euclidean QFT and classical statistical mechanics in $d+1$ dimensions: phase transitions in spin systems map to RG flow in the dual QFT, lattice regularizations of QFT compute thermodynamic quantities, and Monte Carlo methods cross over freely. (1) Wrong sign — Euclidean rotation REGULATES the integral, doesn't make it divergent. (2) The Euclidean integral is mathematically well-defined; unitary Lorentzian results are recovered by analytic continuation back.

questions.q: In QED, the scalar propagator (Feynman gauge, free photon, internal momentum $p$) is:
choices: $i/(p^2 - m^2 + i\epsilon)$ — same form as the scalar propagator with the photon mass set to zero, modulo gauge factors.
$1/(p^2 + m^2)$ — the Euclidean form, no $i\epsilon$.
$\delta(p^2-m^2)$ — only on-shell modes propagate.
$e^{-ip\cdot x}$ — a plane wave, not a Green's function.
questions.hint: The propagator is the Green's function of the free equation of motion. For a massive scalar that's $(\Box+m^2)G(x)=-i\delta^4(x)$; Fourier-transforming gives the momentum-space propagator. The $+i\epsilon$ prescription enforces causal/Feynman boundary conditions.
questions.explain: $i/(p^2-m^2+i\epsilon)$ is the Feynman propagator — the Green's function of $(\Box+m^2)$ with the $+i\epsilon$ contour displacing poles into the lower-left and upper-right of the complex $p^0$ plane, so the contour integration picks up positive-energy modes propagating forward in time and negative-energy modes (=antiparticles) propagating backward. (1) is Euclidean. (2) is the on-shell delta function (LSZ external states), not an internal-line propagator. (3) is a plane wave, not a Green's function.

questions.q: For the QED scattering process $e^+ e^- \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ at tree level, in the high-energy limit $\sqrt s \gg m_\mu$, the cross-section is $\sigma = \frac{4\pi\alpha^2}{3s}$. Using $\alpha = 1/137$ and $\sqrt s = 100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ (so $s = 10^4\,\mathrm{GeV}^2$), what is $\sigma$ in nanobarns? (Use $\hbar c = 0.197\,\mathrm{GeV\cdot fm}$, so $1\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-2} = 0.389\,\mathrm{mb} = 3.89\times 10^5\,\mathrm{nb}$.)
questions.hint: Plug in: $\sigma = (4\pi/3) \cdot (1/137)^2 \cdot (1/10^4\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-2})$ then convert via $1\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-2} = 3.89\times 10^5\,\mathrm{nb}$. The $4\pi/3$ factor traces to integrating $|\mathcal M|^2$ over the muon angular distribution.
questions.explain: $\sigma = (4\pi/3) \times (1/137)^2 \times (1/10^4\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-2}) \approx 4.19 \times 5.33\times 10^{-5} \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-2} \approx 2.23\times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{GeV}^{-2}$. Convert: $\sigma \approx 2.23\times 10^{-8} \times 3.89\times 10^5\,\mathrm{nb} \approx 8.68\times 10^{-3}\times 10\,\mathrm{nb} \approx 0.087\,\mathrm{nb}$. This is the canonical 'point-like' cross-section that benchmarks QCD jets at $e^+e^-$ colliders, and the agreement with PETRA/LEP measurements is one of the cleanest tree-level QED tests.

questions.q: Match each part of a Feynman diagram on the left to what it computes on the right.
right: Quantum correction at order $\hbar^L$ where $L$ is the number of independent loops; introduces a momentum integral $\int d^4k/(2\pi)^4$ that may be UV-divergent.
Asymptotic in/out particle: an on-shell wave function $u(p), v(p), \epsilon^\mu(p)$ from the LSZ formula, on-shell condition $p^2 = m^2$.
Propagator $i/(p^2-m^2+i\epsilon)$ for scalars (or appropriate generalization for fermions/photons); off-shell virtual particle.
Coupling factor from $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{int}}$ — e.g. $-ie\gamma^\mu$ for QED, $ig f^{abc}$ for non-Abelian gauge theory.
questions.hint: Two of the diagram pieces are point-like (interaction terms or scattering endpoints) and two carry momenta (on-shell external, off-shell virtual / loop). Sort by 'Is this on-shell?' first, then by 'Does this introduce an integration?'.
questions.explain: (0)→2: internal lines = propagators, off-shell. (1)→3: vertices = couplings from the interaction Lagrangian. (2)→1: external lines = on-shell wave functions from LSZ. (3)→0: closed loops introduce momentum integrals and are responsible for both the running coupling and the UV divergences that need renormalization. Tree-level diagrams have $L=0$ and recover classical scattering; loops are quantum corrections.

questions.q: The QED beta function at one loop is $\beta(\alpha) = \frac{2\alpha^2}{3\pi}$ (positive). Solving $\mu d\alpha/d\mu = \beta(\alpha)$ between scales $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ shows:
choices: $\alpha(\mu_2) < \alpha(\mu_1)$ for $\mu_2 > \mu_1$ — coupling decreases logarithmically (asymptotic freedom).
$\alpha(\mu_2) > \alpha(\mu_1)$ for $\mu_2 > \mu_1$ — coupling grows logarithmically with energy; vacuum-polarization screening of the bare charge weakens at short distances.
$\alpha$ stays exactly constant — only the bare coupling runs, not the physical one.
$\alpha(\mu)$ blows up at every scale — QED is not a well-defined QFT.
questions.hint: Sign of $\beta$ determines flow direction. $\beta>0$ means the coupling grows as $\mu$ increases; in QED, the physical picture is that virtual electron-positron pairs screen the bare charge, so probing at higher energy (= shorter distance, less screening) sees more bare charge.
questions.explain: Integrating $d\alpha/d\ln\mu = 2\alpha^2/(3\pi)$ gives $1/\alpha(\mu_2) = 1/\alpha(\mu_1) - (2/3\pi)\ln(\mu_2/\mu_1)$. Since the right side decreases with $\mu_2 > \mu_1$, $\alpha(\mu_2) > \alpha(\mu_1)$. Numerically, $\alpha(M_Z) \approx 1/128$ vs $\alpha(0) \approx 1/137$ — the running has been measured at LEP. (3) is the Landau pole: $\alpha$ does diverge at a finite scale (the Landau scale, $\sim 10^{286}\,\mathrm{GeV}$ in pure QED), but it's astronomically far above any physical scale, and embedding QED in the Standard Model fixes it (the U(1)_Y of the SM merges with SU(2)_L).

questions.q: Which of the following are honest statements of the renormalization program? Select all that apply.
choices: Loop integrals like $\int d^4k/k^4$ are UV-divergent; regulators (dim reg, Pauli-Villars, hard cutoff) parametrize the divergence.
Bare couplings $g_0,m_0$ are absorbed into divergent counterterms so that renormalized couplings $g(\mu),m(\mu)$ are finite functions of a sliding scale $\mu$.
A theory is renormalizable when only finitely many couplings are needed to absorb all divergences at every loop order — equivalently, when all interaction vertices have mass-dimension $\le 4$.
Renormalization removes infinities that signal genuine mathematical inconsistency; once renormalized, the theory has no remaining UV sensitivity at any scale.
questions.hint: Three of these are textbook statements; one mischaracterizes what renormalization actually does (especially in light of Wilson's effective-field-theory reframing).
questions.explain: (0,1,2) are the standard story. (3) is wrong on the modern reading: Wilson reframed renormalization as integrating out modes above scale $\Lambda$; the resulting effective theory is sensitive to high-scale physics through the values of low-energy couplings, not through divergences. The 'infinities' aren't inconsistencies — they signal that perturbation theory loses meaning above some scale, and the cure is matching to a UV completion. Even non-renormalizable theories make sense as effective field theories below a cutoff.

questions.q: Order the steps of the renormalization program for a 1-loop divergent diagram in $\phi^4$ theory.
items: Express the renormalized vertex / propagator in terms of the renormalized coupling $g(\mu)$ and finite remainders only.
Compute the 1-loop diagram and find a UV divergence as the regulator is removed.
Choose a regulator: dim reg ($d = 4-\epsilon$), Pauli-Villars, or a hard cutoff $\Lambda$.
Define a renormalization scheme (MS, on-shell, etc.) at scale $\mu$ that fixes the finite parts of the counterterms.
Add counterterms $\delta g, \delta m, \delta Z$ to the Lagrangian so the divergent part of the diagram is canceled.
questions.hint: You can't see the divergence until you've defined what to compute; you can't cancel it until you've isolated it; you need a scheme to know what 'finite' means; only at the end can you write the result in terms of physical (renormalized) couplings.
questions.explain: (2) Regulator first — without one, the integral is formally infinite and you can't manipulate it. (1) Compute, find the divergence as $\epsilon\to 0$ or $\Lambda\to\infty$. (4) Counterterms are designed to cancel the divergence — but their finite parts are scheme-dependent. (3) The scheme fixes the finite remainder. (0) The result is then a finite expression in the renormalized coupling at scale $\mu$. Skipping the scheme (3) would leave the answer ambiguous up to a finite redefinition; that ambiguity is exactly the renormalization-group freedom.

qft-gauge-fields.title: Quantum gauge fields and the Standard Model

questions.q: Promoting a global continuous symmetry $\psi \to e^{i\alpha^a T^a}\psi$ to a local one $\alpha^a = \alpha^a(x)$ in the Lagrangian:
choices: Has no effect — the kinetic term is already invariant.

Forces the introduction of gauge fields $A_\mu^a$ with covariant derivative $D_\mu = \partial_\mu - igA_\mu^a T^a$, transforming as $A_\mu^a \to A_\mu^a + (1/g)\partial_\mu\alpha^a + f^{abc}\alpha^b A_\mu^c$.
Requires breaking Lorentz symmetry to compensate for the $x$-dependent phase.
Allows arbitrary gauge fields with no constraint on their dynamics.
questions.hint: Compute $\partial_\mu(e^{i\alpha(x)T}\psi)$ — does it transform homogeneously, the way the kinetic term needs? If not, what compensating connection $A_\mu$ would make $D_\mu = \partial_\mu - igA_\mu$ transform homogeneously?
questions.explain: $\partial_\mu(e^{i\alpha(x)}\psi) = e^{i\alpha(x)}(\partial_\mu + i\partial_\mu\alpha)\psi$ — the $\partial_\mu\alpha$ piece breaks the global invariance. Introducing $A_\mu \to A_\mu + (1/g)\partial_\mu\alpha$ (Abelian) or its non-Abelian analogue with structure constants $f^{abc}$ exactly cancels this, and the covariant derivative $D_\mu\psi = (\partial_\mu - igA_\mu)\psi$ transforms covariantly. The kinetic term $\bar\psi i\not{D}\psi$ is then locally invariant. This is the gauge principle, the basis of QED ($U(1)$), QCD ($SU(3)$), and electroweak unification ($SU(2)\times U(1)$).

questions.q: Match each Standard Model gauge factor on the left to the gauge bosons it produces on the right.
right: Hypercharge gauge boson $B$, mixing with $W^3$ to give the physical $Z$ and the photon $\gamma$.
Spontaneous electroweak symmetry breaking: gives $W^\pm, Z$ masses and leaves $\gamma$ massless via $\langle\phi\rangle\ne 0$.
8 gluons $G^a_\mu$, $a=1,\ldots,8$, mediating the strong force; self-interacting due to the non-Abelian structure constants of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$.
3 weak bosons $W^1,W^2,W^3$; $W^\pm$ are the linear combinations $W^1\mp iW^2$ that mediate charged-current weak interactions.
questions.hint: Count gauge generators: $\dim\mathfrak{su}(N) = N^2-1$, $\dim\mathfrak{u}(1) = 1$. Match to the boson counts on the right. The Higgs is a mechanism, not a gauge factor — it acts on the previous three.
questions.explain: (0)→2: $\dim\mathfrak{su}(3) = 8$ — 8 gluons, color-charged because $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ is non-Abelian. (1)→3: $\dim\mathfrak{su}(2) = 3$ — three weak bosons; $W^\pm$ are the charged combinations and $W^3$ mixes with $B$. (2)→0: $\dim\mathfrak{u}(1) = 1$ — single hypercharge boson. (3)→1: the Higgs mechanism is the dynamics breaking $\mathrm{SU}(2)_L\times\mathrm{U}(1)_Y\to\mathrm{U}(1)_{\mathrm{em}}$, giving $W^\pm,Z$ masses while preserving renormalizability — and was directly confirmed at the LHC in 2012.

questions.q: Find the error: "In the Higgs mechanism, the Higgs boson gives mass to all gauge bosons. The photon is massive because it couples to the Higgs vacuum expectation value $\langle\phi\rangle\ne 0$, just like the W and Z. The 'masslessness of the photon' you read about is an experimental approximation that breaks down at very low energies."
steps: The Higgs field $\phi$ acquires a vacuum expectation value $\langle\phi\rangle\ne 0$, breaking $\mathrm{SU}(2)_L\times\mathrm{U}(1)_Y$.
Gauge bosons acquire masses from the kinetic term $|D_\mu\phi|^2$ when $\phi$ is replaced by $\langle\phi\rangle$.
The photon, like $W^\pm$ and $Z$, is massive because it couples to $\langle\phi\rangle$.
Experimentally, photons appear massless only as a low-energy approximation that breaks down.
questions.hint: The unbroken subgroup leaves one combination of $W^3$ and $B$ unbroken — that combination doesn't couple to the Higgs vev at all, so it stays massless. Which combination is the photon, and what is its hypercharge with respect to $\langle\phi\rangle$?
questions.explain: Step 2 is the error. The Higgs vev $\langle\phi\rangle$ has electroweak quantum numbers $(I_3,Y) = (-1/2, +1/2)$, so the electric charge $Q = I_3 + Y/2 = 0$ on the vev. The combination of $W^3$ and $B$ that couples to $Q$ is the photon $A_\mu = \sin\theta_W W^3_\mu + \cos\theta_W B_\mu$, and since $Q\langle\phi\rangle = 0$, the photon does NOT couple to the vev and therefore remains exactly massless — the unbroken $\mathrm{U}(1)_{\mathrm{em}}$. Step 3 is also empirically wrong: experimental photon-mass bounds are $m_\gamma < 10^{-18}\,\mathrm{eV}$, indistinguishable from zero. The photon's masslessness is a structural consequence of the Higgs mechanism, not an approximation.
